items.title: The Sahara was a green savannah 6,000 years ago
items.claim: Around 6,000 years ago, what is now the world's largest hot desert was something quite different. What was it?

options.text: It was already a desert; the Sahara has been arid for over 100,000 years
It was a savannah and grassland with lakes, rivers and human settlement — the 'African Humid Period'
It was a tropical rainforest like the Amazon today
It was covered by a shallow sea connected to the Mediterranean

items.reveal:
The African Humid Period lasted roughly 14,500 to 5,000 years ago. Cave paintings at Tassili n'Ajjer in Algeria show people herding cattle, swimming, and hunting hippos.

The cause was an orbital wobble — a stronger summer monsoon driven by changes in Earth's tilt and precession (Milankovitch cycles). When the monsoon retreated, the region desertified rapidly. Lake Chad was once larger than the Caspian Sea ('Lake Megachad').
items.why: Climate zones feel permanent on a human timescale. They are not. The Sahara's transformation in a few millennia is a reminder that 'natural' is just a snapshot of an unstable system.

items.title: Aftershocks can be larger than the original quake
items.claim: What is the technical relationship between a mainshock and aftershocks?

options.text: Aftershocks are always smaller than the mainshock

If a later event is larger than the original, it is retrospectively reclassified as the mainshock and the earlier event becomes a foreshock — so by definition the named mainshock is the largest in the sequence
Aftershocks are unrelated to mainshocks and randomly distributed

items.reveal:
Bath's law gives the largest aftershock as typically 1.2 magnitudes smaller than the mainshock. Omori's law (1894) gives the rate as decaying as 1/t. Aftershocks can continue for years after large events.

The 2011 Christchurch earthquake (magnitude 6.3, 22 February) was an aftershock of the September 2010 Darfield earthquake (7.1). Because the Christchurch event was smaller, it kept the aftershock label — but it killed 185 people because it was shallower and closer to the city.
items.why: Naming conventions can obscure danger. The aftershock label can sound like 'less hazardous' when the geometry of the event matters more than its magnitude.

items.title: Longshore drift can move entire beaches kilometres

options.text: It moves sand offshore into deep water
Wave-driven net sediment transport along the coast in the direction of prevailing waves — building spits (Spurn, Dawlish Warren) and stripping beaches downdrift of groynes
It mixes salt and freshwater at estuaries
It transports sediment upstream in rivers

items.reveal:
Swash hits the beach at an angle (the angle of incoming waves) and backwash returns straight downslope under gravity. Net effect: sediment moves along the coast, often metres per day for fine sand.

Spurn Head (Yorkshire) is a 5 km spit built by longshore drift carrying sediment from Holderness cliffs (eroding at up to 2 m/year) southward. The cliffs supply around 1 million m³ of sediment per year.

Groynes trap drift on their up-drift side and starve beaches on the down-drift side — a coastal management trade-off.
items.why: Coastal protection in one place can damage another. Sediment budgets are zero-sum: a beach kept by groynes is sand denied to the next beach down the coast.
